chapters.title: Chapter 3: Recession Signals in Real Economy Data

lessons.title: Bank Non-Food Credit Growth as a Recession Gauge

body.text: Who is borrowing, and for what, tells you more about where the cycle stands than the aggregate credit growth number. A healthy-looking headline figure can be entirely propped up by retail lending while industrial credit is already decelerating sharply underneath it.

children.text: Chapter 2 covered credit spreads, the price of risk. This lesson covers the quantity side: bank credit growth itself, published fortnightly by the RBI as part of its Sectoral Deployment of Credit data. Aggregate credit growth is a starting point, not an endpoint. The sectoral composition underneath it is where the genuinely useful, early signal sits.
Non-Food vs Food Credit: Why the Distinction Exists

markDefs.definition: Bank lending extended specifically to fund government foodgrain procurement operations, typically through agencies like the Food Corporation of India. It is small relative to total credit, driven by procurement policy and seasonal harvest timing, and largely unrelated to the business cycle.

children.text: Every credit growth figure this course cites, and every one worth citing in practice, is non-food credit growth, not total credit growth.

is small, lumpy, and driven by procurement policy and harvest timing rather than economic conditions. Including it would add noise to the series for no analytical benefit, which is exactly why the RBI itself, and every analyst who uses this data seriously, reports the two figures separately and treats non-food credit growth as the meaningful cyclical indicator.
The Sectoral Breakdown: Where the Credit Is Actually Going

The RBI's Sectoral Deployment of Credit data splits non-food credit into broad categories: Industry (further split by large, medium, and micro and small enterprises), Services, Personal Loans (housing, vehicle, credit card, and other retail lending), and Agriculture. These categories do not move together, and they should not be expected to. Industry credit tracks capex and working capital needs directly, making it highly cyclically sensitive. Personal loans have grown into a genuinely large share of total bank credit over the past decade, as banks have pivoted toward retail lending, partly to diversify away from corporate credit risk. Agriculture credit, like agricultural output itself from Lesson 1.3, is weakly cyclical and driven more by policy and monsoon conditions than by the broader economic cycle.

body.text: Watch for the specific late-cycle pattern where banks lean harder into retail and personal loan growth precisely as corporate demand for credit is softening, propping up the aggregate non-food credit growth number even as industrial credit, the more cyclically honest piece, is already decelerating sharply underneath it. This is the credit-market equivalent of the IIP composition trap from Lesson 3.1.

markDefs.definition: Large, highly rated companies raising funds directly from the bond and money markets, through instruments like commercial paper and non-convertible debentures, instead of borrowing from banks, particularly when market rates are cheaper than bank lending rates.

children.text: Bank credit data has one structural gap worth knowing before relying on it too heavily:

. Large, well-rated corporates increasingly fund themselves through commercial paper (CP) and corporate bonds directly, bypassing bank loans entirely when market rates are favourable. This means bank credit growth increasingly reflects the borrowing needs of mid-market companies, MSMEs, and retail borrowers, who have less access to bond markets, more than it reflects large corporate activity. The RBI addresses this with a broader measure, flow of resources to the commercial sector, which adds CP, corporate bonds, external commercial borrowings, and other financing sources to bank credit, for a fuller picture of total credit flowing into the economy.

body.label: Broader Credit Measure
body.value: Flow of Resources to the Commercial Sector
body.context: Published by the RBI, combining bank credit with commercial paper, corporate bonds, external commercial borrowings, and other sources; useful when large-corporate financing has shifted away from bank loans

children.text: Reading Credit Growth Against the Phase Framework

cells: Expansion
Broad-based acceleration across industry, services, and personal loans together
Peak
Industrial credit growth starts decelerating first, often masked by still-strong personal loan growth in the aggregate figure
Contraction / Deceleration
Broad deceleration spreading to personal loans too, as banks turn risk-averse across the board
Trough
Credit growth stabilises at low levels; retail/personal lending often turns up first as banks compete for the safest category before industrial credit recovers

body.title: Reading a Sectoral Credit Release
steps: Confirm you are looking at non-food credit growth, not the total credit figure, which is distorted by food credit's policy-driven swings
Break the aggregate number down into Industry, Services, Personal Loans, and Agriculture before drawing any conclusion
Check specifically whether Industry credit growth is decelerating even if the aggregate headline still looks healthy
If large-corporate activity is in question, check the RBI's flow of resources to the commercial sector for the fuller picture including CP and corporate bonds
Cross-check the credit growth read against the AA-minus-AAA credit spread differential from Lesson 2.2 for a consistent risk-appetite signal

body.title: Decompose the Aggregate
body.scenario: Aggregate non-food credit growth is reported at a healthy-looking 14% year-on-year. Digging into the sectoral breakdown, Industry credit growth has decelerated sharply to 4%, from 12% a year earlier, while Personal Loans grew 22% over the same period, and Services credit grew a moderate 11%.
body.prompt: Is the headline 14% figure a reliable signal that credit conditions are healthy across the economy? What is it actually telling you?
body.modelAnswer: No, the headline figure is misleading on its own. It is being propped up almost entirely by 22% personal loan growth, while Industry credit, the most cyclically sensitive category by this lesson's framework, has decelerated from 12% to just 4%, a sharp slowdown that the aggregate number almost completely hides. This is the exact late-cycle pattern flagged earlier in this lesson: banks leaning into retail lending as corporate credit demand weakens. The correct read is that credit conditions for businesses, particularly the capex and working-capital-driven part of the economy, are cooling meaningfully, even though the number a casual reader would see in a headline still looks reassuring. This would be worth cross-checking against Industry-specific data like capital goods IIP growth from Lesson 3.1 and credit spreads from Lesson 2.2 to see whether the same deceleration shows up there too.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: Why can bank credit data alone understate financing activity for large, highly rated corporates specifically?
options: Because large corporates are not permitted to borrow from banks at all

Because disintermediation means large, well-rated companies increasingly raise funds directly through commercial paper and corporate bonds rather than bank loans, especially when market rates are cheaper
Because the RBI does not track credit extended to large companies
Because large corporates only borrow in foreign currency
body.explanation: Disintermediation, large corporates bypassing banks in favour of directly raising funds through CP and corporate bonds when market rates are favourable, means bank credit growth increasingly reflects mid-market, MSME, and retail borrowing more than large-corporate activity, which is why the RBI's broader flow of resources to the commercial sector measure exists as a supplement.

body.text: This lesson presents a general framework for reading sectoral credit data, for educational purposes. Figures used in examples are illustrative. Always check the RBI's current Sectoral Deployment of Credit and Flow of Resources to the Commercial Sector releases for actual data. Nothing here is investment advice.

points: Non-food credit growth, not total credit growth, is the meaningful cyclical figure; food credit is small, policy-driven, and unrelated to the business cycle
Industry credit is the most cyclically sensitive category and often decelerates first, sometimes masked in the aggregate by still-strong personal loan growth, a late-cycle pattern worth watching for
Disintermediation means large corporates increasingly bypass bank loans for CP and corporate bonds, which is why the RBI's flow of resources to the commercial sector gives a fuller financing picture
Credit composition has its own phase signature: broad-based in expansion, industry-led deceleration at peak, broad deceleration in contraction, and retail-led stabilisation at the trough
The next lesson closes Chapter 3 by turning to corporate earnings, the most lagging piece of real-economy data this course covers, and why it still matters despite arriving last
